I have farmed these 6 mu in Quzhou County my whole life. I never went to school, but the land taught me everything I need to know. Here on the North China Plain, there is only one sensible way to farm: winter wheat and summer corn, year after year. My wheat went into the ground last October after the autumn rains, and now that the soil is thawing, I am already thinking about the first irrigation and the urea top-dressing. I will spread about 40 jin of urea per mu on the wheat when it greens up, just like my neighbors do, and I put down compound fertilizer at planting. The wheat will need four good waterings and four sprays for bugs and weeds. In early June, when the wheat is cut, I will plant hybrid corn the very same day—there is no time to plow between crops, so I plant directly into the stubble. The corn needs less fertilizer than the wheat, just some compound at planting and urea at the jointing stage, with two irrigations and three pesticide sprays if the weather stays dry. I do not bother with cotton or vegetables—those are too much work and too risky. Wheat and corn are what the grain station buys, and they are what feed my family.
